title: Rethinking Structured Generation: Can Graph-Based Reasoning Resolve Ambiguity?
claim: Resolve input ambiguity by generating several candidate outputs, converting each to a graph, and selecting the best through joint reasoning.
layout: 5 stages, left-to-right, numbered captions below, color-coded candidate rows
description: A five-stage left-to-right pipeline with numbered labels along the bottom. At far left, a cartoon person with a thought bubble ('???') and a scroll quoting 'Sales increased in summer and declined in winter.' Red text reads 'Season? Time? Sales?', and the caption says natural language is inherently ambiguous. An arrow leads to stacked, color-coded candidate tables: orange for season-level, blue for month-level, green for 'other interpretation', separated by dots. Each candidate has a matching colored graph, such as a 'Sales Trend' root node linked to Summer/Winter or Jun/Jul/Dec leaves with Increase/Decrease edges. All the graphs feed into a large blue 'Reasoning Module' with network icons and three criteria boxes: relational consistency, semantic coherence and structural validity. Blue arrows then lead to ranked output cards with medal badges 1, 2 and 3. The eye lands first on the colorful tables and then follows the arrows rightward.
caption: Overview of the proposed ambiguity-aware structured generation framework. Given an ambiguous natural-language input, the model first generates multiple candidate structured representations capturing different plausible interpretations. Each candidate is then converted into a graph encoding task-specific entities and their relationships. A graph-based reasoning module evaluates and compares the candidates based on semantic coherence, structural validity, and relational consistency, enabling principled selection beyond token-level likelihoods. Finally, the candidates are ranked and the highest-scoring structure is selected as the output.
abstract: Structured generation is typically formulated as a deterministic mapping from input to a single structured output. This assumption is fundamentally misaligned with natural language, which often admits multiple structurally distinct yet semantically valid interpretations. As a result, existing methods rely on single-reference supervision that collapses ambiguity into one prediction, leading to unstable and inconsistent outputs under underspecified inputs. We reformulate structured generation as an \textit{ambiguity-aware inference problem}, where the objective is to reason over a set of plausible structured outputs rather than predict a single solution. We show that standard training inherently suppresses valid alternatives, and instead adopt a multi-valid learning framework that preserves ambiguity during optimization. To operationalize this formulation, we construct a candidate space of structured outputs, represent each candidate as a graph capturing entities and their relationships, and perform selection via graph-based reasoning over semantic alignment and relational consistency. This enables principled comparison across competing interpretations beyond token-level likelihoods. Experiments on structured generation benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in accuracy, stability, and robustness under varying levels of ambiguity. These results highlight the importance of modeling ambiguity explicitly and suggest a shift from single-output prediction to set-level reasoning in structured generation.
